text: AI is often encouraging.
It can praise your essay, support your idea,
and agree with your opinion.
Even when what you really need is honest criticism.
The flattery trap is treating AI's approval
as honest evaluation.
You ask an AI to evaluate this introduction
for a great Gatsby essay.
You write that the American dream
is something people have thought about.
Some achieve it, some don't,
and Fitzgerald explores this idea.
The AI can take two paths here.
The first is flattery.
It says, great start.
You've clearly identified the central theme.
This is a strong foundation.
It praises the work without pointing to any evidence,
resulting in false praise for a weak intro.
The second path is useful feedback.
It says, right topic, but this needs work.
The opening is filler and you still need a thesis.
It praises the specific topic,
names the missing thesis,
and gives you a specific next move.
Good feedback improves the actual work.
It can still be positive
as long as it points to real evidence in the text,
but empty praise only improves the feeling.
Here's why AI leans agreeable.
One reason is a training process
called reinforcement learning from human feedback,
or RLHF.
In this process, human reviewers
compare different answers and choose the ones they prefer.
Positive, confident, and agreeable answers
can feel better in the moment.
So those responses win approval.
The training algorithm pushes the model
toward these highly approved agreeable patterns.
The praise literally gets baked into the system.
The technical name for this behavior is sycovancy.
AI agrees with or praises the user
instead of giving an honest answer.
In April 2025, a user tested chat GPT
by pitching an absurd gag product, poop on a stick.
Here is how the AI responded.
It generated glowing over the top praise,
saying, honestly, this is absolutely brilliant.
It's genius.
It even called the ridiculous gift, performance art.
Open AI began rolling that specific update back
three days after it launched,
publicly identifying the behavior as sycovancy.
But researchers have found this same pattern
across multiple AI assistants, not just chat GPT.
AI companies actively test for sycovancy now
and use system instructions to reduce it.
The problem has improved,
but it has not entirely disappeared.
How you ask still matters.
Here are three ways to fight the flattery trap.
First, ask, don't tell.
If you say, I think this plan is good,
thoughts, you give the AI your opinion
before it evaluates the work.
Instead, prompt it with evaluate this plan
before I tell you what I think.
Share the work, but hold back your own verdict.
Second, ask for the gaps.
Asking, is my essay good,
is a broad request for approval.
A cheerful yes does not tell you what to revise.
Instead, ask, what's weak, what's missing,
and what would someone who disagrees say?
Now you have given the AI specific things to look for.
Third, use a rubric.
Without a supplied standard, AI guesses the criteria.
Telling it to simply grade my essay isn't enough.
Instead, tell it, grade it against this rubric,
quote the evidence, and show how to move up one level.
Keep in mind, asking it to quote evidence
ties the feedback to your actual writing,
but the response is still just a guide.
It is something to check against your work,
not an official guarantee of accuracy or a final grade.
In applications that support it,
you can save this direction to guide all future responses,
so you don't have to type it every time.
Be direct with me, lead with what needs work,
point to specific evidence, and tell me when I'm wrong.
Ask AI to improve the work, not approve of you.
Look for specifics, not approval.
